claims.claim: The coiled-coil region of Hip1 family members can homo-heterodimerize and also binds clathrin light chain.
claims.source: The coiled-coil region can homo-heterodimerize and also binds clathrin light chain (Engqvist-Goldstein et al., 2001; Metzler et al., 2001; Legendre-Guillemin et al., 2002; Gottfried et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Engqvist-Goldstein et al., 2001; Metzler et al., 2001; Legendre-Guillemin et al., 2002; Gottfried et al., 2010.

claims.claim: The THATCH domain is an actin-binding module.
claims.source: The THATCH domain is an actin-binding module (Yang et al., 1999; Engqvist-Goldstein et al., 2001; Brett et al., 2006; Wilbur et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Yang et al., 1999; Engqvist-Goldstein et al., 2001; Brett et al., 2006; Wilbur et al., 2008.

claims.claim: Sla2/Hip1R binds actin and is thought to function as a major link between the clathrin coat and actin.
claims.source: Accordingly, Sla2/Hip1R binds actin and is thought to function as a major link between the clathrin coat and actin.
claims.evidence: This is based on the actin-binding properties of the THATCH domain and prior studies.

claims.claim: Studies in yeast have shown that the ENTH domain of epsin and the ANTH domain of Sla2 interact with each other.
claims.source: Studies in yeast have additionally shown that the ENTH domain of epsin and the ANTH domain of Sla2 interact with each other, and the two proteins function together in providing a link between the endocytic coat and the actin cytoskeleton (Skruzny et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Skruzny et al., 2012.

claims.claim: The two proteins (epsin and Sla2) function together in providing a link between the endocytic coat and the actin cytoskeleton.
claims.source: Studies in yeast have additionally shown that the ENTH domain of epsin and the ANTH domain of Sla2 interact with each other, and the two proteins function together in providing a link between the endocytic coat and the actin cytoskeleton (Skruzny et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Skruzny et al., 2012.

claims.claim: In vitro studies showed that the amphipathic helix of the ENTH domain confers the property to induce bilayer curvature and even to fragment bilayer tubules into vesicles.
claims.source: In vitro studies showed that this helix confers, upon the ENTH domain, the property to induce bilayer curvature and even to fragment bilayer tubules into vesicles, thus pointing to a potential role of the epsin in fission (Itoh et al., 2001; Ford et al., 2002; Boucrot et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Itoh et al., 2001; Ford et al., 2002; Boucrot et al., 2012.

claims.claim: The germline knockout of the mouse Epn1 and Epn2 genes did not block early embryonic development.
claims.source: Surprisingly, in view of this evidence for an important housekeeping role of epsin in endocytosis, the germline knockout (KO) of the mouse Epn1 and Epn2 genes that encode the two major ubiquitously expressed mammalian epsins, epsin 1 and 2, did not block the early embryonic development (Chen et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2009.

claims.claim: Arrest of embryonic development in Epn1 and Epn2 double KO mice occurred only at E9.5–E10, with a pattern suggestive of impaired Notch signaling.
claims.source: Arrest of embryonic development occurred only at E9.5–E10, with a pattern suggestive of impaired Notch signaling, while no obvious defects in clathrin-mediated endocytosis were observed in fibroblasts derived from these embryos (Chen et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2009.

claims.claim: No obvious defects in clathrin-mediated endocytosis were observed in fibroblasts derived from Epn1 and Epn2 double KO embryos.
claims.source: Arrest of embryonic development occurred only at E9.5–E10, with a pattern suggestive of impaired Notch signaling, while no obvious defects in clathrin-mediated endocytosis were observed in fibroblasts derived from these embryos (Chen et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2009.

claims.claim: Studies of epsin 1 and 2 conditional double KO endothelial cells revealed a selective defect in the internalization of ubiquitinated VEGF receptor.
claims.source: Moreover, studies of epsin 1 and 2 conditional double KO endothelial cells revealed a selective defect in the internalization of ubiquitinated VEGF receptor (Pasula et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Pasula et al., 2012.

claims.claim: A recent study based on RNAi-mediated knock-down in fibroblastic cells reported that the KD of all three epsins produces a global impairment of clathrin-mediated endocytosis, which was attributed to a defect of the fission reaction.
claims.source: However, a recent study based on RNAi-mediated knock-down (KD) in fibroblastic cells reported that the KD of all the three epsins produces a global impairment of clathrin-mediated endocytosis, which was attributed to a defect of the fission reaction (Boucrot et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Boucrot et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Epn1loxP/loxP; Epn2−/−; Epn3−/− animals were viable and fertile with no obvious pathological phenotypes.
claims.source: Epn1loxP/loxP (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, see also [Pasula et al., 2012]) mice were crossed with Epn2 (Chen et al., 2009) and Epn3 KO (Ko et al., 2010) mice to generate Epn1loxP/loxP; Epn2−/−; Epn3−/− animals, which were viable and fertile with no obvious pathological phenotypes.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claims.claim: Epn1loxP/loxP; Epn2−/−; Epn3−/−; Cre-ER+/0 animals did not exhibit obvious defects.
claims.source: These mice were subsequently interbred with mice transgenic for 4-hydroxy-tamoxifen (OHT)-inducible Cre recombinase [Cre-ER, Badea et al., 2003] to obtain Epn1loxP/loxP; Epn2−/−; Epn3−/−; Cre-ER+/0 animals. These mice did not exhibit obvious defects either.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claims.claim: Immunoblotting demonstrated the near complete disappearance of epsin 1 from conditional TKO cell extracts in response to OHT.
claims.source: Immunoblotting with epsin isoform-specific antibodies demonstrated the near complete disappearance of epsin 1 from conditional TKO cell extracts in response to OHT (Figure 1A) and confirmed the absence of epsin 2 and 3 (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Immunoblotting confirmed the absence of epsin 2 and 3 in conditional TKO cells.
claims.source: Immunoblotting with epsin isoform-specific antibodies demonstrated the near complete disappearance of epsin 1 from conditional TKO cell extracts in response to OHT (Figure 1A) and confirmed the absence of epsin 2 and 3 (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: A C-terminal epsin 2 fragment (MW about 40 kDa) was detected in cells containing the epsin 2 KO allele, possibly reflecting an alternative start site.
claims.source: A C-terminal epsin 2 fragment (MW about 40 kDa) was detected in cells containing the epsin 2 KO allele, possibly reflecting an alternative start site (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: The KD of the C-terminal epsin 2 fragment by RNAi in TKO cells did not produce phenotypic changes in addition to the ones described.
claims.source: However, the KD of this fragment by RNAi in TKO cells did not produce phenotypic changes in addition to the ones described below, indicating that it does not play a relevant role.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claims.claim: OHT-dependent loss of epsin 1 expression was validated by anti-epsin 1 immunofluorescence, as the typical punctate epsin 1 signal was completely absent.
claims.source: OHT-dependent loss of epsin 1 expression was also validated by the anti-epsin 1 immunofluorescence, as the typical punctate epsin 1 signal (reflecting clathrin-coated pits [Chen et al., 1998]) was completely absent (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: Nestin-Cre epsin TKO animals were born, but at a lower than expected Mendelian ratio.
claims.source: Nestin-Cre epsin TKO animals were born, but at a lower than expected Mendelian ratio.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claims.claim: A few days after birth, nestin-Cre epsin TKO animals began to develop locomotor dysfunction, failed to gain weight, and rapidly deteriorated, typically dying before the end of the fourth week.
claims.source: A few days after birth they began to develop locomotor dysfunction, failed to gain weight (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), and rapidly deteriorated, typically dying before the end of the fourth week.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Western blot analysis of extracts of nestin-Cre epsin TKO brains at the beginning of the fourth week confirmed the absence of all three epsin genes.
claims.source: Western blot analysis of extracts of their brains at the beginning of the fourth week, confirmed the absence of all the three epsin genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: TKO MEFs were abnormally large compared to WT cells.
claims.source: Microscopy of the TKO MEFs revealed them to be abnormally large compared to WT cells (contour in Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: TKO cells contained multiple clustered nuclei or very large and abnormally shaped nuclei.
claims.source: Furthermore, these cells contained multiple clustered nuclei or very large and abnormally shaped nuclei, as shown by both DAPI staining and Cre immunofluorescence (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,F), in contrast to the single nuclei present in the smaller WT cells.
claims.evidence: Supported by DAPI staining and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,F.

claims.claim: The abnormal nuclei in TKO cells could be explained by the reported role of epsin 1 and 2 in mitotic spindle organization.
claims.source: This finding could be explained by the reported role of epsin 1 and 2 in mitotic spindle organization (Liu and Zheng, 2009), a defect that can result in abnormal chromosome segregation and impaired cytokinesis.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Liu and Zheng, 2009.

claims.claim: Analysis of WT and TKO cells during 48-hours of OHT treatment revealed that the increase in either cell size or size/number of nuclei of TKO cells was accompanied by a strong cell number reduction.
claims.source: Accordingly, analysis of WT and TKO cells during 48-hours of OHT treatment revealed that the increase in either cell size or size/number of nuclei of TKO cells was accompanied by a strong cell number reduction (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: Immunostaining of cells synchronized by double-thymidine treatment for anti-Aurora B kinase showed a striking decrease of cytokinesis profiles in TKO.
claims.source: Additionally, immunostaining of cells synchronized by double-thymidine treatment (Banfalvi, 2011) for anti-Aurora B kinase, a marker of midbodies of telophase ([Banerjee et al., 2014] inset of Figure 1D), showed a striking decrease of cytokinesis profiles in TKO (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: Immunostaining of TKO cells for α-adaptin and clathrin-light chain showed an increase in the density of clathrin-coated pits relative to controls.
claims.source: Immunostaining of TKO cells for α-adaptin (a subunit of the clathrin adaptor complex AP-2) and for clathrin-light chain (CLC) showed an increase in the density of clathrin-coated pits relative to controls (Figure 2A–D).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2A–D.

claims.claim: Most pits in TKO cells occurred in small clusters rather than as single-puncta.
claims.source: Additionally, most pits occurred in small clusters rather than as single-puncta (insets in Figure 2A–D).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2A–D.

claims.claim: Total levels of clathrin and α-adaptin were not changed in TKO cells.
claims.source: Total levels of clathrin and α-adaptin, however, were not changed (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that the increase in pits reflects an increase in the pool of assembled clathrin coats (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The increase in pits in TKO cells reflects an increase in the pool of assembled clathrin coats.
claims.source: Total levels of clathrin and α-adaptin, however, were not changed (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that the increase in pits reflects an increase in the pool of assembled clathrin coats (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that total levels are unchanged but pit density is increased.

claims.claim: Live imaging with spinning disk confocal microscopy of cells transfected with μ2-adaptin-GFP revealed that the turnover rate of pits in TKO cells was much lower than in WT cells.
claims.source: Clathrin-coated pit dynamic was also altered, as live imaging with spinning disk confocal microscopy of cells transfected with μ2-adaptin-GFP (another subunit of the AP-2 complex) revealed that the turnover rate of pits in TKO cells was much lower than in WT cells (Figure 2F,G).
claims.evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 2F,G.

claims.claim: An impairment of the internalization of fluorescent transferrin was observed in TKO cells.
claims.source: In agreement with these morphological changes, an impairment of the internalization of fluorescent transferrin, a cargo of endocytic clathrin-coated pits, was also observed in TKO cells.
claims.evidence: Supported by transferrin uptake assay data shown in Figure 2H,I.

claims.claim: Following preincubation with Alexa594-transferrin on ice and subsequent incubation at 37°C for 15 min, the bulk of transferrin remained at the cell surface in TKO cells, while remaining transferrin was intracellular in control cells.
claims.source: Following preincubation with Alexa594-transferrin on ice and subsequent incubation at 37°C for 15 min, the bulk of transferrin remained at the cell surface in TKO cells, while remaining transferrin was intracellular in control cells (Figure 2H,I).
claims.evidence: Supported by transferrin uptake assay data shown in Figure 2H,I.

claims.claim: A major shift of overexpressed and endogenous transferrin receptor from a punctate localization in the cytoplasm (WT cells) to a plasma membrane localization (TKO cells) was observed.
claims.source: This change correlated with a major shift of overexpressed and endogenous transferrin receptor from a punctate localization in the cytoplasm (WT cells) to a plasma membrane localization (TKO cells), as demonstrated by both immunofluorescence (Figure 2J,K) and a cell surface biotinylation assay (Figure 2L).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2J,K and biotinylation assay data shown in Figure 2L.

claims.claim: Transferrin internalization impairment could be rescued by electroporation of epsin1-GFP cDNA.
claims.source: Transferrin internalization impairment could be rescued by electroporation of epsin1-GFP cDNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D).
claims.evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D.

claims.claim: A major shift of the localization of synaptobrevin 2/VAMP2 (Syb2) was observed in TKO MEFs stably expressing Syb2-HA.
claims.source: Likewise, a major shift of the localization of synaptobrevin 2/VAMP2 (Syb2), a vesicular SNARE that is internalized by clathrin-mediated endocytosis, was observed in TKO MEFs stably expressing Syb2-HA, (this construct harbors the HA epitope at the very short C-terminal non-cytosolic portion of Syb2).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence and biotinylation assay data shown in Figure 2M-R.

claims.claim: Total Syb2 immunoreactivity had a predominant punctate intracellular distribution in control MEFs, and an additional strong plasma membrane localization in TKO.
claims.source: Total Syb2 immunoreactivity had a predominant punctate intracellular distribution in control MEFs, and an additional strong plasma membrane localization in TKO (Figure 2M,O).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2M,O.

claims.claim: The presence of an abundant surface exposed pool of Syb2 selectively in TKO MEFs was confirmed by surface immunofluorescence for the HA epitope and by a cell surface biotinylation assay.
claims.source: The presence of an abundant surface exposed pool of Syb2 selectively in TKO MEFs was confirmed by the surface immunofluorescence for the HA epitope (Figure 2N,P) and by a cell surface biotinylation assay (Figure 2Q,R).
claims.evidence: Supported by surface immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2N,P and biotinylation assay data shown in Figure 2Q,R.

claims.claim: When cells were examined by electron microscopy, the major increase in TKO cells was observed for shallow and U-shaped pits.
claims.source: When cells were examined by electron microscopy to assess the stage at which clathrin-mediated endocytosis is impaired in TKO cells, the major increase was observed for shallow and U-shaped pits (Figure 2S,T).
claims.evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2S,T.

claims.claim: Multiheaded-coated structures could reflect clustering of shallow/intermediate stage pits at the pre-fission stage.
claims.source: However, multiheaded-coated structures, which were not clearly detected in our cells (Figure 2S,T), could instead reflect clustering of shallow/intermediate stage pits at the pre-fission stage.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claims.claim: Dynamin 2, endophillin 2, and myosin 1E were present at the subset of very late pits in WT cells, while in TKO cells they had a diffuse cytosolic distribution.
claims.source: In agreement with an arrest at early stage, dynamin 2, endophillin 2, and myosin 1E (a myosin implicated in clathrin-mediated endocytosis [Cheng et al., 2012]), three proteins whose localization at pits peaks at the time of fission (Taylor et al., 2011) were present at the subset of very late pits in WT cells, while in TKO cells they had a diffuse cytosolic distribution (Figure 2U).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2U.

claims.claim: Phalloidin staining for F-actin revealed only few of the actin stress fibers typically observed in control cells.
claims.source: Phalloidin staining for F-actin revealed only few of the actin stress fibers typically observed in control cells (Figure 3A,B) and a strong accumulation of F-actin foci in TKO cells (Figure 3B,D), sometimes in the form of elongated curved structure at the cell cortex (inset in Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: Supported by phalloidin staining data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claims.claim: A strong accumulation of F-actin foci was observed in TKO cells.
claims.source: Phalloidin staining for F-actin revealed only few of the actin stress fibers typically observed in control cells (Figure 3A,B) and a strong accumulation of F-actin foci in TKO cells (Figure 3B,D), sometimes in the form of elongated curved structure at the cell cortex (inset in Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: Supported by phalloidin staining data shown in Figure 3B,D.

claims.claim: Similar results were observed upon immunostaining for Arp 2/3.
claims.source: Similar results were observed upon immunostaining for Arp 2/3 (an actin nucleating complex that functions with N-WASP [Figure 3E]).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: A difference in actin organization relative to WT cells was observed by live TIRF microscopy of TKO cells, co-expressing CHUtr–mCh and CLC–GFP, as there was a general increase in the pool of actin associated with clathrin spots.
claims.source: A difference in actin organization relative to WT cells was also observed by live total internal reflection (TIRF) microscopy of TKO cells, co-expressing the calponin homology domain of utrophin fused to mCherry (CHUtr–mCh) and CLC fused to GFP (CLC–GFP), as there was a general increase in the pool of actin associated with clathrin spots (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: Supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: The expression of full-length epsin1–GFP rescued actin cytoskeleton changes.
claims.source: The expression of full-length epsin1–GFP (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D) rescued actin cytoskeleton changes (Figure 3C,D).
claims.evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claims.claim: No significant alterations of the levels of several major components of the clathrin-dependent endocytic machinery were observed in TKO cells.
claims.source: Interestingly, while no significant alterations of the levels of several major components of the clathrin-dependent endocytic machinery were observed in TKO cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), the level of Hip1R was increased (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The level of Hip1R was increased in TKO cells.
claims.source: Interestingly, while no significant alterations of the levels of several major components of the clathrin-dependent endocytic machinery were observed in TKO cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), the level of Hip1R was increased (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Pull down experiments from rat brain homogenate, using ENTH–GST or GST alone as bait, showed the affinity-purification of Hip1R in the presence of diC8-PI(4,5)P2.
claims.source: Pull-down experiments from rat brain homogenate, using ENTH domain of epsin 1 as bait revealed an enrichment of Hip1R in the affinity-purified material in the sample also containing PI(4,5)P2 (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: Supported by pull-down experiment data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The typical clathrin-coated pit-like punctate localization of endogenous and exogenous Hip1R was replaced in TKO cells by a diffuse signal.
claims.source: Additionally, the typical clathrin-coated pit-like punctate localization (Engqvist-Goldstein et al., 1999) of endogenous (immunofluorescence, Figure 4C) and exogenous (TIRF microscopy of Hip1R-GFP, Figure 4F) Hip1R was replaced in TKO cells by a diffuse signal (Figure 4D,F).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4C,D and TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: Expression of epsin1-GFP in TKO cells rescued Hip1R localization.
claims.source: Expression of epsin1-GFP in TKO cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D) rescued Hip1R localization (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: The localization of epsin at pits was independent of Hip1R, as Hip1R KD in HeLa cells by RNAi did not affect epsin localization.
claims.source: In contrast, the localization of epsin at pits was independent of Hip1R, as Hip1R KD in HeLa cells by RNAi (Figure 4G) did not affect epsin localization (Figure 4H).
claims.evidence: Supported by RNAi knockdown experiment data shown in Figure 4G,H.

claims.claim: Upon incubation with WT mouse brain cytosol and nucleotides, growth of tubular invaginations was revealed in en face views by the resulting GFP puncta.
claims.source: Plasma membranes obtained by sonication of PTK2 cells expressing PM-anchored GFP exhibit a homogeneous fluorescence when kept in cytosolic buffer (Wu and De Camilli, 2012). Upon incubation with WT mouse brain cytosol and nucleotides, growth of the tubular invaginations was revealed in en face views by the resulting GFP puncta (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), and 'in side' views by the growth of short columns of GFP fluorescence perpendicular to the plane of the coverslip (Figure 5A, left PM-GFP panel).
claims.evidence: Supported by cell-free assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and Figure 5A.

claims.claim: The presence of clathrin at the tips of the tubules was confirmed by immunofluorescence.
claims.source: The presence of clathrin at the tips of the tubules was confirmed by immunofluorescence (Figure 5A, left clathrin panel).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Epsin immunoreactivity precisely overlapped with clathrin indicating epsin localization throughout the clathrin coat.
claims.source: Epsin immunoreactivity precisely overlapped with clathrin (Figure 5A, left epsin panel) indicating epsin localization throughout the clathrin coat.
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Clathrin-capped invaginations also formed on plasma membrane sheets incubated with epsin TKO brain cytosol.
claims.source: Clathrin-capped invaginations also formed on plasma membrane sheets incubated with epsin TKO brain cytosol (Figure 5A, right panels and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: Supported by cell-free assay data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: In membrane sheets incubated with control brain cytosol, F-actin polymerized in alignment with the invaginations thus generating a well-organized scaffold that contributes to maintain their parallel orientation perpendicular to the plasma membrane.
claims.source: In membrane sheets incubated with control brain cytosol, F-actin polymerized in alignment with the invaginations thus generating a well-organized scaffold that contributes to maintain their parallel orientation perpendicular to the plasma membrane (Figure 5B, left panels).
claims.evidence: Supported by cell-free assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: In membranes incubated with TKO cytosol, the F-actin network around the invaginations was exaggerated and disorganized.
claims.source: On the contrary, in membranes incubated with TKO cytosol, the F-actin network around the invaginations was exaggerated and disorganized (Figure 5B, right panels), leading to clumping of the tips of the invaginations in a meshwork of actin.
claims.evidence: Supported by cell-free assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: As a result of the disorganized actin network, invaginations often had an oblique orientation in TKO cytosol incubations.
claims.source: As a result of this clumping, invaginations often had an oblique orientation (Figure 5A,B, right panels and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: Supported by cell-free assay data shown in Figure 5A,B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Regularly spaced cross-sectioned tubules interspersed within an actin meshwork were observed with WT cytosol, but numerous obliquely cut tubules embedded in a dense actin matrix were visible with TKO cytosol.
claims.source: Such disorganization was confirmed by electron microscopic observations of sections cut parallel to the substrate. Regularly spaced cross-sectioned tubules interspersed within an actin meshwork were observed with WT cytosol, but numerous obliquely cut tubules embedded in a dense actin matrix were visible with TKO cytosol (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D).
claims.evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D.

claims.claim: Myosin 1E was localized at the bottom of the tubular invaginations in sheets incubated with WT cytosol, but at the tips in sheets incubated with epsin TKO brain cytosol.
claims.source: Another striking modification related to an abnormal actin cytoskeleton was the mislocalization of myosin 1E. As shown by immunofluorescence, this protein was localized at the bottom of the tubular invaginations in sheets incubated with WT cytosol, but at the tips in sheets incubated with epsin TKO brain cytosol (Figure 5C and higher magnifications).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Hip1R immunoreactivity was present at the tips of the invaginations in sheet preparations incubated with WT cytosol, but was largely absent from the tubules incubated with TKO cytosol.
claims.source: Furthermore, in agreement with these observations, Hip1R immunoreactivity was present at the tips of the invaginations in sheet preparations incubated with WT cytosol, but was largely absent from the tubules incubated with TKO cytosol (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Hip1R levels were higher in TKO brain cytosol in agreement with the higher levels of Hip1R in TKO fibroblasts.
claims.source: This was in spite of the higher levels of Hip1R in the TKO brain cytosol (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E) in agreement with the higher levels of Hip1R in TKO fibroblasts (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E and Figure 4A.

claims.claim: When membrane sheets were incubated with Hip1/Hip1R DKO brain cytosol, differences from WT were observed that were qualitatively similar to those obtained with the epsin TKO cytosol, but quantitatively milder.
claims.source: When membrane sheets were incubated with Hip1/Hip1R DKO brain cytosol, differences from WT were observed that were qualitatively similar to those obtained with the epsin TKO cytosol, but quantitatively milder (Figure 5E,F).
claims.evidence: Supported by cell-free assay data shown in Figure 5E,F.

claims.claim: Localization of epsin 1 at the tips of the invaginations was not affected by the absence of Hip1/Hip1R in the cytosol.
claims.source: Importantly, localization of epsin 1 at the tips of the invaginations was not affected by the absence of Hip1/Hip1R in the cytosol (Figure 5G), once again as in the case of intact cells.
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: Both the DPW and NPF motif containing regions of epsin, but not the ENTH domain, bind actin.
claims.source: This analysis revealed that both the DPW and NPF motif containing regions of the protein (Chen et al., 1998), but not the ENTH domain, bind actin (Figure 5H).
claims.evidence: Supported by co-sedimentation assay data shown in Figure 5H.

claims.claim: There appear to be at least two actin-binding sites in epsin.
claims.source: Thus, there appear to be at least two actin-binding sites in epsin.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that both DPW and NPF regions bind actin.

claims.claim: The site in the NPF motif containing region likely corresponds to the actin cytoskeleton-binding (ACB) site, previously identified in yeast epsin (Ent1).
claims.source: The site in the NPF motif containing region likely corresponds to the actin cytoskeleton-binding (ACB) site, previously identified in yeast epsin (Ent1, Skruzny et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Skruzny et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Pull-downs from mouse brain lysate using GST–ENTH domain of epsin 1 as bait, followed by analysis of the affinity purified material by mass spectroscopy, identified Syb2 as one of the top hits.
claims.source: Pull-downs from mouse brain lysate using GST–ENTH domain of epsin 1 as bait, followed by analysis of the affinity purified material by mass spectroscopy, identified Syb2 as one of the top hits (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The very low affinity of the interaction between the ENTH domain of epsin 1 and the cytosolic portion of Syb2 (KD 470 ± 30 μM) was enhanced by the presence of IP6 (KD 80 ± 7.9 μM).
claims.source: The very low affinity of this interaction (KD 470 ± 30 μM) was enhanced by the presence in the incubation medium of IP6 (KD 80 ± 7.9 μM, Figure 6B,D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), which induces the folding of helix zero of the ENTH domain (Itoh et al., 2001; Ford et al., 2002).

results.result: Conditional epsin triple knockout (TKO) mice and cells were successfully generated using a tamoxifen-inducible Cre system, resulting in near-complete loss of all three epsin isoforms as confirmed by immunoblotting and immunofluorescence.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C34 and C37 collectively demonstrate successful generation of conditional TKO mice and cells with validated loss of epsin expression through multiple complementary methods (immunoblotting in Figures 1A-B and immunofluorescence in Figure 1C). The experimental approach is well-documented and the results are internally consistent.

results.result: Epsin TKO cells display dramatic cell division defects including abnormally large cell size, multiple or abnormally shaped nuclei, reduced cell proliferation, and decreased cytokinesis events.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C41-C45, and C119 are supported by multiple lines of evidence including microscopy (Figure 1C-D), cell counting (Figure 1E), and Aurora B kinase staining (Figure 1F). The phenotypes are consistent with the reported role of epsin in mitotic spindle organization (C43), though the mechanistic basis is not fully explored in this study.

results.result: Epsin TKO cells show a robust impairment in clathrin-mediated endocytosis with accumulation of shallow and U-shaped clathrin-coated pits, indicating that epsin's most critical function is at the transition between early and deeply invaginated pits.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C46-C50, C58, C117, and C131 are strongly supported by immunofluorescence (Figure 2A-D), live imaging (Figure 2F-G), and electron microscopy (Figure 2S-T). The electron microscopy data directly demonstrates accumulation of shallow/U-shaped pits, and the absence of late-stage markers (C60) at pits further supports an early-stage arrest. This is a central finding of the manuscript.

results.result: Transferrin internalization is impaired in epsin TKO cells, with transferrin and its receptor accumulating at the plasma membrane rather than being internalized, and this defect can be rescued by epsin1-GFP expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C54 are supported by transferrin uptake assays (Figure 2H-I), immunofluorescence (Figure 2J-K), biotinylation assays (Figure 2L), and rescue experiments (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-D). The rescue experiment (C54) provides strong evidence that the phenotype is specifically due to loss of epsin.

results.result: Synaptobrevin 2/VAMP2 (Syb2) shows increased surface localization in epsin TKO cells, indicating impaired internalization of this vesicular SNARE protein.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C57 are supported by total and surface immunofluorescence (Figure 2M-P) and biotinylation assays (Figure 2Q-R) in cells stably expressing Syb2-HA. The convergent evidence from multiple assays strongly supports increased surface accumulation of Syb2 in TKO cells.

results.result: Late-stage endocytic proteins (dynamin 2, endophillin 2, myosin 1E) show diffuse cytosolic distribution in TKO cells rather than punctate localization at clathrin-coated pits.
results.evaluation: Claim C60 is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2U showing loss of punctate localization for all three late-stage markers. This is consistent with the arrest at early stages of pit maturation and provides additional evidence for the stage at which epsin function is critical.

results.result: Epsin TKO cells show disrupted actin cytoskeleton organization with loss of stress fibers and accumulation of F-actin foci at the cell surface, particularly near arrested clathrin-coated pits, which can be rescued by epsin1-GFP expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C61-C65, and C98 are supported by phalloidin staining (Figure 3A-B), Arp2/3 immunostaining (Figure 3E), TIRF microscopy (Figure 3F), and rescue experiments (Figure 3C-D). The convergent evidence from multiple approaches and the rescue experiment strongly support the conclusion that epsin is required for proper actin organization at endocytic sites.

results.result: Hip1R levels are increased in epsin TKO cells, but Hip1R fails to localize to clathrin-coated pits in the absence of epsin, while epsin localization is independent of Hip1R.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C71 and C97 are supported by immunoblotting (Figure 4A), pull-down assays (Figure 4B), immunofluorescence (Figure 4C-E), TIRF microscopy (Figure 4F), and RNAi experiments (Figure 4G-H). The data clearly demonstrate that epsin is required for Hip1R recruitment to pits, but not vice versa, establishing a hierarchical relationship between these proteins.

results.result: In a cell-free assay using plasma membrane sheets, epsin-deficient cytosol produces clathrin-capped invaginations with exaggerated and disorganized F-actin networks compared to wild-type cytosol.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C79 and C100 are supported by confocal microscopy (Figure 5A-B) and electron microscopy (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-D) of the cell-free assay. The data clearly show that while clathrin-coated structures form with TKO cytosol, the actin organization is severely disrupted, providing direct evidence for epsin's role in coordinating actin dynamics with endocytic coat assembly.

results.result: In the cell-free assay, myosin 1E is mislocalized to the tips rather than the base of invaginations with TKO cytosol, and Hip1R is largely absent from invaginations despite increased levels in TKO cytosol.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C82 are supported by immunofluorescence data from the cell-free assay (Figure 5C-D) and immunoblotting (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E). The mislocalization of myosin 1E and absence of Hip1R from invaginations despite increased total levels provides strong evidence for epsin's role in organizing the spatial distribution of actin-related proteins.

results.result: Hip1/Hip1R double knockout cytosol produces qualitatively similar but quantitatively milder defects compared to epsin TKO cytosol in the cell-free assay, and epsin localization is not affected by absence of Hip1/Hip1R.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C84 are supported by cell-free assay data (Figure 5E-G) showing that Hip1/Hip1R DKO produces intermediate phenotypes and that epsin localization is maintained. This establishes that while Hip1R and epsin function together, epsin has additional functions beyond recruiting Hip1R.

results.result: Epsin binds actin directly through its disordered tail region, with at least two actin-binding sites in the DPW and NPF motif-containing regions, but not the ENTH domain.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C87 and C99 are supported by co-sedimentation assays (Figure 5H) showing direct binding of epsin tail fragments to F-actin. The identification of two binding sites and the connection to the yeast ACB site (C87) provides mechanistic insight into how epsin couples to actin.

results.result: Epsin's ENTH domain binds synaptobrevin 2/VAMP2 with low affinity (KD ~470 μM, enhanced to ~80 μM by IP6) through the N-terminal portion of Syb2's SNARE motif and helix zero of the ENTH domain, and this interaction is evolutionarily conserved.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C95, C6, and C112 are supported by mass spectrometry (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), pull-down assays with quantitative binding measurements (Figure 6A-D), deletion analysis (Figure 6C, E-I), co-immunoprecipitation from intact cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C-E), and yeast protein binding (Figure 6J). The low affinity is well-characterized with KD measurements, and the evolutionary conservation is demonstrated.

results.result: Epsin's key evolutionary conserved function is to orchestrate coupling between actin and endocytic clathrin coats that limits excessive actin growth and helps mediate the effect of actin polymerization on bud invagination, ultimately generating force for invagination and fission.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C96, C101, and C129 represent the main conclusions drawn from the collective experimental evidence. These are well-supported by the convergent data from TKO cells (Figures 2-4), cell-free assays (Figure 5), and direct actin binding (Figure 5H). The conclusion that epsin coordinates actin-coat coupling is strongly supported, though the specific contribution to fission (C5) is more inferential.

results.result: Brain-specific nestin-Cre epsin TKO mice are born at sub-Mendelian ratios, develop locomotor dysfunction and fail to thrive, typically dying before 4 weeks of age, with confirmed absence of all three epsins in brain tissue.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C40 are supported by phenotypic observations and Western blot analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D-E). While these mice were not the primary focus of the study, the data clearly demonstrate that complete loss of epsins in the brain is incompatible with normal postnatal development.

results.result: A C-terminal epsin 2 fragment (~40 kDa) is detected in epsin 2 KO cells, possibly from an alternative start site, but RNAi knockdown of this fragment does not produce additional phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C36 are supported by immunoblotting (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) and RNAi experiments. The authors appropriately tested whether this fragment has functional significance and found it does not contribute to the observed phenotypes, validating that the TKO is functionally complete.

results.result: The excess actin nucleation in epsin-deficient cells may be explained by epsin's interaction with Cdc42-GAPs, as yeast epsins bind Rga1/Rga2 and mammalian epsin binds RLIP76/RalBP1, which could modulate N-WASP-Arp2/3-dependent actin nucleation.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C104 are based on prior literature (citations to Aguilar et al., 2006 and Rossé et al., 2003) and represent a speculative mechanistic explanation (C104 is explicitly labeled as speculation). While the hypothesis is reasonable and consistent with the observed phenotypes, no direct experimental evidence is provided in this study to test the role of Cdc42-GAP interactions in the observed actin phenotypes.

results.result: Epsin's requirement for Notch signaling may be linked to its role in controlling actin dynamics at clathrin-coated pits, as Notch activation requires pulling force from ligand endocytosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C109 are based on prior literature, while C110 is an inference connecting the current findings to Notch signaling. While the hypothesis is plausible given the demonstrated role of epsin in actin-dependent endocytosis, no direct experiments testing Notch signaling in the TKO cells are presented. This remains a reasonable but untested hypothesis.

results.result: The very low affinity binding of synaptobrevin 2 to epsin may be physiologically relevant when compounded with epsin's other interactions with the bilayer, coat components, and cargo proteins, potentially collaborating with AP180/CALM to couple bud nucleation to SNARE incorporation.
results.evaluation: Claims C115 and C127 are explicitly speculative hypotheses about the physiological significance of the low-affinity Syb2-epsin interaction. While the interaction is well-documented (C88-C95), the functional significance and cooperation with AP180/CALM are not directly tested. The accumulation of Syb2 at the surface in TKO cells (C55-C57) is consistent with but does not prove this hypothesis.

results.result: The absence of major cell division defects in epsin 1 and 2 double KO embryonic fibroblasts may be due to long-term adaptation, such as upregulation of epsin 3.
results.evaluation: Claim C120 is speculative and C121 refers to unpublished observations. While the hypothesis of compensatory upregulation is reasonable and could explain the difference between acute (TKO) and chronic (DKO) epsin loss, the evidence is incomplete and not formally presented. This represents an interesting observation that would require additional validation.

results.result: Multiheaded-coated structures observed in prior RNAi studies could reflect clustering of shallow/intermediate stage pits at the pre-fission stage rather than a fission defect.
results.evaluation: Claim C59 is explicitly speculative and represents an alternative interpretation of structures observed in prior studies (Boucrot et al., 2012) that were not clearly detected in the current study. While this interpretation is plausible, it is not directly tested and represents a reinterpretation of others' data rather than a primary finding.

results.result: Actin polymerization force may help drive deep invagination and assist dynamin-dependent fission, and epsin's helix zero membrane insertion properties may assist dynamin in fission.
results.evaluation: Claims C106 and C130 are partially speculative (C106 and C130 both include speculation in their evidence types). While supported by prior literature (citations to Itoh et al., 2005 and Roux et al., 2006), the specific contribution of epsin to fission is not directly demonstrated in this study. The accumulation of shallow pits (C58) suggests the primary defect is earlier than fission, making the fission role less certain.

results.result: Epsin's role in cytoskeleton dynamics may underlie its function in mitosis, for example by affecting anchoring to the cell cortex.
results.evaluation: Claim C123 is explicitly speculative and represents a hypothesis connecting the observed actin phenotypes to the mitotic defects. While plausible given the demonstrated role in actin organization, no direct experiments testing this mechanism in mitosis are presented. The mitotic phenotypes are documented but not mechanistically explored.

results.result: Background information on epsin structure, function, and prior genetic studies in various organisms, including its domains, binding partners, and roles in endocytosis and Notch signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C7-C30, C92, C105, C113-C114, C122, and C125 represent background information from the literature, supported by numerous citations. These claims establish the context for the current study and are appropriately referenced. They are not primary findings of this manuscript but are accurately represented summaries of prior work.

results.result: Levels of several major clathrin-dependent endocytic machinery components are not significantly altered in epsin TKO cells.
results.evaluation: Claim C66 is supported by immunoblotting data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) showing unchanged levels of clathrin, α-adaptin, and caveolin. This control experiment is important for establishing that the observed phenotypes are not due to general disruption of endocytic protein expression.

results.result: Total cellular levels of clathrin and α-adaptin are unchanged in epsin TKO cells.
results.evaluation: Claim C48 is supported by immunoblotting (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) and is important for interpreting the increased pit density (C46) as reflecting increased assembly rather than increased protein expression. This is a key control supporting the interpretation of the morphological data.
